title: Penguins name franchise legend Ron Francis as special advisor of hockey operations
content:
PITTSBURGH – Ron Francis and the Penguins have always been a perfect match.

They’re together again.

Francis, a Hockey Hall of Famer and one of the greatest players in franchise history, has returned to Pittsburgh as a special advisor for hockey operations. The Penguins announced the news Friday.

“Ron has a deep affinity for the city of Pittsburgh and the Penguins. He cherishes his time spent here as a player, where he had tremendous success and is an outstanding ambassador for the Penguins and the city of Pittsburgh,” Kyle Dubas, the Penguins’ president of hockey operations and general manager, said in a statement. “Ron’s playing experience, management experience, and familiarity with the Penguins and Pittsburgh will be a great benefit to our organization and all members of our management team.”

Like Dubas, Francis is a native of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.

Previously, Francis was general manager of the Carolina Hurricanes from 2014-18, replacing Jim Rutherford. He was also the first general manager in Seattle Kraken history.

While Francis, 63, spent much of his legendary playing career in Hartford and Raleigh, his name is carved on the Stanley Cup twice as a player with the Penguins. One of the biggest names on one of the biggest-named teams in hockey history, Francis was a two-way force on the Penguins’ 1991 and 1992 Stanley Cup champion teams. The Penguins acquired him in the most famous trade in franchise history on March 4, 1991, which made the team an immediate Stanley Cup contender.

Francis is considered one of the most cerebral players ever and ranks fifth in NHL history with 1,798 points, a total that is only surpassed by Wayne Gretzky, Jaromir Jagr, Mark Messier and Gordie Howe. He was at his very best with the Penguins.

Over eight seasons with the Penguins, Francis produced 613 points in 533 games, a gaudy 1.15 points per game average, while subsequently having the reputation for being one of hockey’s best defensive forwards. He served as Penguins captain in the 1994-95 season, when Mario Lemieux took a season off for health reasons, and again in the 1997-98 season after Lemieux’s first retirement.

Francis is widely considered one of the greatest players and most respected people in Penguins history.

While Francis only enjoyed modest success as a general manager in Carolina and Seattle, he is highly regarded around the NHL for his hockey savvy.

Francis’ addition is also relevant in other organizational avenues:

• The Penguins are hopeful that Jaromir Jagr will become more of a regular in Pittsburgh and perhaps even join the organization in some capacity in the future. Francis was Jagr’s center almost exclusively for the final five years of their time as teammates in Pittsburgh, and the two have a strong relationship.

• The Penguins love having their most beloved former players in the organization, and Francis’ presence — no matter how heavy or light it may be — will be welcome.

• The Penguins are hopeful that Mario Lemieux will play some role when the Hoffmann Family officially takes over the franchise, which is expected to happen at some point in the next few weeks. Francis and Lemieux are very close.

Aside from these tidbits, though, the Penguins are clearly pleased to have an executive with Francis’ experience and intelligence joining the organization.
